list.listitem: Serum screening for pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A) and free beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) with nuchal translucency measurement is an effective first-trimester screen for Down syndrome. Offer invasive genetic testing, either chorionic villus sampling (CVS) or amniocentesis, to women with positive screens. A

Integration of first- and second-trimester screening methods increases the detection rate and decreases the false-positive rate. Cell-free DNA is the most sensitive screening test, but still has some limintations. B ,

Patients with Down syndrome require newborn cardiac evaluation and annual screening of thyroid function, CBC, vision, hearing, symptoms of constipation, and sleep apnea. Order radiograph for atlantoaxial instability once between the ages 3 and 5 years, or whenever there is a neurologic complaint or neurologic physical examination finding. C
Use GLOBAL Medical Care Guidelines for Adults with Down Syndrome Checklist to support the health of adults with Down syndrome directly or through their caregivers. C
With better medical care and social support, many patients with Down syndrome are surviving into adulthood and are living full and increasingly independent lives. C

background.definition: Down syndrome is a syndrome of intellectual disability and various physical malformations due to excess material from chromosome 21.

list.listitem: 1/700 live births in the US. Incidence is higher among mothers with advanced maternal age (see ).
Compared with non-Hispanic white mothers, the risk ratio for non-Hispanic Black mothers is 0.77 and for Hispanic mothers it is 1.12.
The number of individuals in the U.S. with Down syndrome is estimated at between 200,000 to 250,000 with about half that number being adults.

Children with Down syndrome are at higher risk for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). In one large U.S. military health system database study, children with Down syndrome had a higher hospitalization rate for RSV (9.6% vs. 2.7%) with greater illness severity based on length of stay (4 days vs. 2 days) and required respiratory support. Children with Down syndrome were also older at time of hospital stay (median age 9.8 months vs. 3.5 months).

Individuals with Down syndrome may be more susceptible to COVID-19 and are at higher risk for severe disease.
Additionally, an observational study suggests that patients with Down syndrome have a decreased antibody response to the mRNA vaccination.

Among children with childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia, Down syndrome was the most significant risk factor for infection-related mortality (OR 12.08; 95% CI 6.54-22.32) even during maintenance therapy.

Epilepsy is highly prevalent in individuals with Down syndrome; a pooled estimate based on data from 13 studies was 12.4% (95% CI 9.1-16.7); prevalence rate was 10.3% (95% CI 8.4-12.6) if the two studies of older adults were removed. Prevalence increased with age, especially in those with Alzheimer's/dementia.

Based on two expert panel English-language literature reviews of papers available through PubMed, individuals with Down syndrome are at higher risk of sleep apnea (up to 85%), hearing impairment (up to 73%), degenerative cervical spine change or spondylosis (33%-64%), congenital heart disease (33%, about half undiagnosed and most frequently mitral, aortic, and tricuspid valve regurgitation), hypothyroidism (27%) and possibly hyperthyroidism (3%), atlantoaxial instability (15%-20% in children), hip dysplasia (5%-20%), and possibly osteoporosis. Menopause occurred about 2 years early among women with Down syndrome and rates of diabetes (4%-8%) and obesity (38%) were similar to the US population, although the rate of obesity in females was 43%.

Anemia may also be more prevalent; in one single-center cohort study of 200 patients with Down syndrome, 22.5% had a hemoglobin concentration less than 2 SDs for normed age, including a rate of 18.7% among children aged 1 to 5 years compared to the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (2007-2010) reported anemia prevalence for children of 3.2%.

A condition referred to as arthropathy of Down syndrome (A-DS) has been reported, consisting of significant polyarticular joint damage/erosive changes, especially in the small joints of the hands and wrists, and associated disability. Based on a screening cohort of 503 children with Down syndrome, 33 (6.6%) were identified with A-DS, including 18 new cases. Prevalence estimates were 20/1000 and erosive changes were reported on X-ray in 42% of children with A-DS compared to 14% with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA). Rheumatoid factor and anti-nuclear antibody are typically negative. In a survey of rheumatologists, most (73%) believed this condition to be identical to JIA and the most used treatments were nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (94%), methotrexate (91%), and anti-TNF agents (90%).
Ninety-five percent due to nonfamilial trisomy 21.
Three percent to 4% due to unbalanced translocation.
One percent to 2% due to genetic mosaicism of one normal cell line and one with trisomy of chromosome 21.
Extra chromosomal material results in varying degrees of intellectual disability and similar phenotypic appearance.
First-trimester screening with PAPP-A, free beta-subunit HCG, and nuchal translucency is as effective as the second-trimester quadruple screen for Down syndrome detection. A
Fully integrated screening, which combines testing from both first and second trimesters to determine risk, is more sensitive than first-trimester screening alone. B

Contingent testing offers invasive genetic testing to women with high-risk first-trimester screens, no further testing to those with low-risk first-trimester screens, and further second-trimester serum testing to those with moderate risk. This also appears to be cost effective. B

Infants and young children with Down syndrome and hemodynamically significant heart disease should be given RSV prophylaxis with palivizumab during RSV season. B The American Academy of Pediatrics found insufficient evidence to recommend prophylaxis for all children with Down syndrome.

Offer all pregnant women, regardless of age, aneuploidy screening before 20 weeks of gestation. Several screening options are available including the first-trimester combined test, the second-trimester quadruple screen, and various integrated tests. Cochrane authors found that tests including two or more markers in combination with maternal age were significantly more sensitive than those with one marker; the value of combining four or more tests or including inhibin is unproven.

The "first-trimester combined test" is performed between 11 and 13 weeks of gestation and includes serum PAPP-A, serum free beta-subunit HCG, and ultrasound nuchal translucency measurements, all of which are converted to multiples of median and adjusted for maternal age and race to determine risk. Detection rate is 85%, with a false-positive rate of 5%.

Nuchal translucency refers to a fluid-filled nuchal space visualized by ultrasound between gestational age 11 and 14 weeks. The technique, with appropriate standardization and quality assurance, may be most useful in multiple gestation pregnancies, when serum markers are not reliable. An abnormal first trimester nuchal translucency with normal karyotype and normal second trimester ultrasound is not associated with adverse neonatal outcome or developmental delay in childhood.

Cochrane authors found that test strategies combining ultrasound markers with serum markers and maternal age were significantly better than those involving only ultrasound markers (with or without maternal age) except nasal bone; absence of nasal bone had a high diagnostic accuracy, but only five out of 10 affected pregnancies with Down syndrome were detected at a 1% false positive rate.

The "second-trimester quadruple screen" is performed between 15 and 18 weeks of gestation and includes serum alpha-fetoprotein, total HCG, unconjugated estriol, and inhibin A; all are adjusted for maternal age to determine risk. Offer this screen to patients who present in the second trimester.

Cochrane authors found that first trimester nuchal translucency and PAPP-A and second trimester total hCG, uE3, AFP and Inhibin A combined with maternal age outperformed other testing strategies, detecting about nine out of every 10 Down syndrome pregnancies at a 5% false positive rate.

Integrated testing involves testing in both trimesters. The fully integrated test uses the combined test results from the first trimester and the quadruple screen results from the second trimester to determine risk, without early disclosure of first-trimester results. Although this combination increases detection rate and decreases the false-positive rate, the disadvantage is that patients do not have screening results until the second trimester. Where nuchal translucency ultrasound is not available, serum testing alone may be obtained in both trimesters resulting in higher detection rates than in either trimester alone.

Sequential testing may be done for patients who prefer to have results earlier in the pregnancy. Patients who are considered high risk after first-trimester testing are offered genetic testing at that time (CVS), and those at low or moderate risk have serum testing in the second trimester. Sequential testing has a 95% detection rate, with a 2.5% false-positive rate.

Contingent testing offers invasive genetic testing to those with high-risk first-trimester screens, no further testing to those with low-risk first-trimester screens, and second trimester serum testing to those with moderate risk. This cost-effective model allows for early diagnosis for higher risk pregnancy with a small increase in false-positive rates compared with sequential testing. In a population study of over 10,000 pregnant women, the optimal first trimester cut-offs were 1:30 (lower cut-off) and 1:900 (upper cut-off), which yielded a rate of 12% of women requiring a second trimester test, with an overall detection rate of 93% and false positive rate of 2.8% for Down syndrome.

A study conducted at 35 international centers with over 15,000 patients tested at a mean gestational age of 12.5 weeks found that cfDNA had higher sensitivity, a lower false positive rate, and higher positive predictive value compared to standard testing with nuchal translucency and biochemical analytes. In this study, the area under the curve for trisomy 21 was 0.999 for cfDNA testing vs. 0.958 for standard screening; all 38 women with trisomy 12 were detected using cfDNA vs. 30/38 with standard testing.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies on cfDNA found a pooled sensitivity of 99.3% and pooled specificity of 99.9% for Down syndrome. They estimated that for each 100,000 pregnancies, cfDNA would detect 417 cases of Down syndrome with 94 false positives (.094%).

A prospective study of nearly 1000 twin pregnancies found that cfDNA testing is the most accurate screening test for trisomy 21 in twin pregnancies with a <0.5% failure rate. Pooled data from 5598 twin pregnancies showed a trisomy 21 detection rate of 95% and false positive rate of 0.1%.

Urine testing is available but has undergone only limited testing; similar to serum markers Cochrane authors found tests including two markers (second trimester ß-core fragment and estriol) in combination with maternal age were significantly more sensitive than those with one marker with maternal age.

Infants and young children with Down syndrome and hemodynamically significant heart disease should be given RSV prophylaxis with palivizumab during the RSV season. Palivizumab is administered intramuscularly at a dosage of 15 mg/kg once a month for a maximum of 5 doses.

This author suggests that all infants and young children with Down syndrome be considered for RSV prophylaxis during the RSV season. In a Dutch study, children with Down syndrome receiving prophylaxis had a 3.6-fold reduction in the incidence rate ratio for RSV-related hospitalization during the first 2 years of life.

In a Japanese cohort study (2007-2015) of 632 children ≤24 months of age with Down syndrome, administration of palivizumab during RSV season significantly reduced RSV‐related hospitalization (16/384 [4.2%] for patients with prophylaxis vs. 15/248 [6%] for patients without prophylaxis; odds ratio 0.41; 95% CI 0.18-0.92).
When prenatal testing or the infant's phenotype suggests a diagnosis of Down syndrome, karyotyping must be done to evaluate for trisomy or translocation of chromosome 21. C
Evaluation for hearing, thyroid, cardiac, visual, and hematologic problems is recommended in the newborn period. C
Although phenotype can vary, several physical features help to distinguish Down syndrome.
Monitor growth using Down syndrome-specific growth charts.

Monitor weight as children with Down syndrome have a higher risk of overweight and obesity; in a Dutch study, rates of overweight and obesity were about double for children with Down syndrome compared with the general population.

Elicit history regarding symptoms of sleep apnea at annual visits, with referral to a sleep medicine specialist as indicated by symptoms. Some experts recommend baseline sleep study in the absence of symptoms at age 4 years.
General: hypotonia.

HEENT: small brachycephalic head, epicanthic folds, flat nasal bridge, upward slanting palpebral fissures, Brushfield spots (small, slightly elevated white spots on the surface of the iris arranged in a concentric ring around the pupil; present in one third to three quarters of individuals with Down syndrome), small mouth, small ears, excessive skin at the nape of the neck.

Vision: Perform developmentally appropriate vision screening including evaluation for strabismus, cataracts, and nystagmus by 6 months of age. Referral to a pediatric ophthalmologist is recommended before 6 months of age because of the increased risk for visual problems. Perform an ophthalmologic evaluation annually in school-aged children.
Extremity: single transverse palmar crease, short fifth finger with clinodactyly, wide space between first and second toes.

Development: variable mental impairment; mild (IQ: 50-70) to moderate (IQ: 35-50) and occasionally severe (IQ: 20-35). Data suggest that for IQ tests, raw scores rather than standardized scores may be more useful for tracking change in cognitive ability over time. Motor function can be assessed using several motor scales including the Alberta Infant Motor Scale, Test of Infant Motor Performance, BAYLEY, Peabody Gross Motor Scale, Gross Motor Function Measure, Movement Assessment Battery for Children and Pediatric Evaluation of Disability Inventory.
Assess degree of cognitive delay in patients with a mental age of 5 years or greater using NIH-Toolbox Cognitive Battery.
Patients with Down syndrome are at increased risk for early onset of Alzheimer's disease. Consider screening for dementia in patients exhibiting symptoms of memory loss or confusion.
See for incidence of various major congenital malformations.
When prenatal testing or the infant's phenotype suggests a diagnosis of Down syndrome, karyotyping must be done to evaluate for trisomy or translocation of chromosome 21.

Perform an objective hearing screen at birth or by 3 months of age (ie, brainstem auditory evoked response [ABR] or otoacoustic emission). Perform an audiogram every 6 months up to 3 years of age or when a pure tone is heard, with referral to an otolaryngologist as needed, and then audiologic evaluation annually. Patients with Down syndrome have a 50% to 70% risk of serous otitis media between the ages 3 and 5 years, which may rarely lead to hearing loss.

Refer to a cardiologist for echocardiogram in the newborn period to evaluate for congenital heart defects. Up to 50% may have congenital cardiac defects, some of which may not be detectable on prenatal ultrasound.
Order a CBC in the newborn period and annually, as Down syndrome is associated with increased risk for leukemia, leukemoid reaction, and polycythemia.

Screen for thyroid disease using thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) in the newborn period as well as at 6 months, 12 months, and then annually due to increased risk for hypothyroidism, which is sometimes subclinical.

Screen for celiac disease at 2 years of age and repeat as indicated by symptoms. History of significant constipation warrants GI referral for evaluation of Hirschsprung's disease, as patients with Down syndrome are at increased risk.

Order screening radiographs to evaluate for atlantoaxial instability or subluxation between the ages of 3 and 5 years (required for Special Olympics participation). Order MRI evaluation for patients with neurologic symptoms.

Screen for Down syndrome using serum PAPP-A and Beta-HCG along with ultrasound for nuchal translucency. Women with positive screens should be offered first trimester CVS or second-trimester amniocentesis. Other options include integrated first- and second-semester screening methods that increase the detection rate and decrease the false-positive rate.

When Down syndrome is suspected clinically or based on karyotype, order echocardiogram, TSH, hearing and vision screen, and a CBC. Other testing to order around age 2 to 3 years, includes screening cervical spine radiographs and serologic testing for celiac disease.
See for long-term monitoring recommendations.
Physical therapy and speech and occupational therapy can help patients with Down syndrome achieve milestones earlier and more effectively. B
There may be academic and social benefit to mainstream schooling for some higher functioning children with Down syndrome. C
Use GLOBAL Medical Care Guidelines for Adults with Down Syndrome Checklist to support the health of adults with Down syndrome directly or through their caregivers. C

Despite the hypothesis that oxidative stress contributes to premature neuronal degeneration in patients with Down syndrome, dietary supplementation with antioxidants and/or folinic acid, a reduced folic acid, has not been shown to alter psychomotor or language development in children with Down syndrome.

Based on two RCTs, memantine was not better than placebo in preventing or treating dementia in patients with Down syndrome. Authors of a Cochrane review were unable to determine the usefulness of pharmacologic treatment to prevent cognitive decline in people with Down syndrome due to low quality evidence.
PT, including early treadmill therapy, results in earlier walking for infants with Down syndrome.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 9 RCTS found positive results for use of strength and balance training on strength of upper and lower limbs (standardized mean difference [SMD] 1.46; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.77-2.15; and SMD 2.04; 95% CI 1.07-3.01, respectively) and mediolateral oscillations of balance (SMD -3.30; 95% CI -5.34 to -1.26).

In a small three-arm trial of 45 4 to 6-year-olds with Down syndrome, all three interventions – traditional PT, PT plus core stability exercise, and PT plus treadmill exercise – resulted in significant improvement in functional balance and stability.
Patients with feeding difficulties benefit from early occupational therapy and dental interventions.
Because oral-motor dysfunction (along with hearing loss) contributes to speech delay and language impairment, early referral to speech therapy is beneficial for children with Down syndrome.
Integrated occupational therapy approaches are an effective treatment for the sensory dysfunction that is common in Down syndrome.

A Cochrane review concluded that there is insufficient evidence to support improved physical or psychosocial outcomes from aerobic exercise in adults with Down syndrome. The studies in the meta-analysis demonstrated improvements in some physiologic measures of performance with exercise.

Authors of a systematic review of 11 studies concluded that exercise interventions were more effective than control conditions for improving static balance of children with Down syndrome and the static-dynamic balance of children and adolescents with Down syndrome, but findings on dynamic balance in children and static balance in adolescents were inconclusive.
Twelve weeks of swim training was not effective in improving respiratory aspects of speech production.

Learning to ride a 2-wheel bicycle was possible for about half of children (aged 8-15 years) with Down syndrome and resulted in significantly less time spent in sedentary activity more time spent in moderate to vigorous physical activity compared to control subjects at 12 months.
Authors of a meta-analysis of 7 studies found that neuromuscular training could be beneficial to improve muscular strength and possibly mobility in children and young adults with Down syndrome.
In a small RCT, whole-body vibration improved balance and muscle strength in children with Down syndrome.
Surveillance for common pediatric complications is recommended (see ).
Use GLOBAL Medical Care Guidelines for Adults with Down Syndrome Checklist to support the health of adults with Down syndrome directly or through their caregivers.
Congenital cardiac abnormality, usually an endocardial cushion defect, is found in up to 50% of children with Down syndrome. Surgical correction significantly improves survival.
In a Swedish case series of 206 newborns with Down syndrome, 47% had congenital heart disease, 11.2% had GI abnormalities, 3.9% had neonatal cholestasis, and 3.4% had bone marrow disease.

For adults with Down syndrome without a history of ASCVD, the appropriateness of statin therapy should be assessed every 5 years starting at age 40 and using a 10-year risk calculator, as recommended for adults without Down syndrome by the USPSTF.
For adults with Down syndrome, risk factors for stroke should be managed as specified by the AHA/ASA guidelines for the primary prevention of stroke.

In adults with Down syndrome with a history of congenital heart disease, given the elevated risk of cardioembolic stroke, a periodic cardiac evaluation and a corresponding monitoring plan should be reviewed by a cardiologist.

Men with Down syndrome are generally infertile, but there have been numerous reports of successful pregnancies in women with Down syndrome. There is a case report of a 36-year-old man with proved non-mosaic trisomy 21 who fathered two normal boys so infertility should not be assumed.

Little is written about sexuality and reproductive health in individuals with Down syndrome. Although this author (MS) found a statement that at least half of women with Down syndrome were fertile, I was unable to find supporting data. Assuming this is true, discussions about contraceptive needs should be conducted as appropriate and contraceptive advice and medication/devices provided.

Medical professionals should assess adults with Down syndrome and interview their primary caregivers about the changes from baseline function annually beginning at age 40. The National Task Group Early Detection Screen for Dementia should be used to identify early-stage age-related Alzheimer-type dementia and/or potentially reversible medical conditions.

Alzheimer's disease and its complications are the leading cause of death in adults with Down syndrome. In this population, the disease follows predictable preclinical biomarker changes over more than two decades, making this population a suitable target for Alzheimer's disease preventive treatments.

Down syndrome is associated with early onset of neuropathologic features of Alzheimer's disease, which manifest clinically as decline in social functioning. There are no data to support use of rivastigmine, memantine, galantamine, donepezil for dementia in people with Down syndrome.

Authors of one review suggest that micro-dose lithium (300 µg daily in one study) may have a role in preventing cognitive decline in patients with Down syndrome and mild cognitive impairment. Further study is needed.
Use caution when diagnosing age-related, Alzheimer-type dementia in adults with Down syndrome younger than 40 years because of its low prevalence before this age.

In a case series of 138 Swedish children with Down syndrome undergoing polysomnography for suspected OSA, 82.6% were confirmed and 39.9% had severe OSA. Improvement was seen in apnea hypopnea index and mean OSA-18 rating for the 20 children undergoing either adenotonsillectomy or adenopharyngoplasty.

In a case series of children with Down syndrome and mild OSA, at 10.5 to 14 months follow-up, there were no differences in the apnea hypopnea index, oxygen nadir, or end-tidal carbon dioxide from baseline to follow-up for the 16 children, median age 4 years, in the observation group compared to the 29 children, median age 7.4 years, in the medication group (intranasal corticosteroids and/or montelukast). This result was confirmed in a second case series of 24 children, 10 of whom were treated with medication. In this study, OSA resolved in one patient treated with observation and two treated with medication, but worsened in two children from each group.

Addressing disturbed sleep is important both for function and quality of life; in addition, in one study there was an association between length of night-time awakenings and striatal beta amyloid, an early pathologic feature of Alzheimer’s disease, and decreased cognitive performance in executive functioning and motor planning and coordination.

In patients with Down syndrome, OSA is commonly identified in the first year of life. Early screening is recommended, especially for those with an NICU stay, feeding difficulties, or airway abnormalities.

Common ear, nose and throat problems affecting people with Down syndrome include hearing issues (often from otitis media with effusion), sleep-disordered breathing, and recurrent upper respiratory tract infections.

Individuals with Down syndrome also have a high incidence of early onset aggressive periodontal disease, higher levels of periodontal pathogens, periodontitis-associated interproximal bone loss, and untreated dental caries. Refer early to a dentist.

Based on a 10-year retrospective study of 101 patients with Down syndrome from a single academic dermatology center, the most common dermatologic conditions were folliculitis (30.7%), seborrheic dermatitis (26.7%) and hidradenitis suppurativa (22.8%).

Authors of a systematic review identified 38 cases with Down syndrome who had BBD. Functional constipation (90%), recurrent urinary tract infections (38%) and enuresis (56%) were common at presentation and 56% required surgical intervention.

A United Kingdom systematic review revealed that patients with Down syndrome have an increased risk of celiac disease and should be offered serologic screening via human leucocyte antigen combined with immunoglobulin A tissue transglutaminase.

When concern for a mental health disorder in adults with Down syndrome is present, medical professionals should refer to a clinician knowledgeable about the medical, mental health, and common behavioral disorders and characteristics of adults with Down syndrome. Follow guidelines for diagnosis in the DSM-5. The DM-ID-2 also may be used to adapt diagnostic criteria from the DSM-5.
There may be academic benefit to mainstream schooling of some higher functioning children with Down syndrome.
Numeracy skills can be improved in children with Down syndrome through twice weekly numerical skills training.
For asymptomatic adults with Down syndrome, screening for type 2 diabetes using HbA1c or fasting plasma glucose should be performed every 3 years beginning at age 30 years.
For any adult with Down syndrome and comorbid obesity, screening for type 2 diabetes using HbA1c or fasting plasma glucose should be performed every 2 to 3 years beginning at age 21 years.

Monitoring for weight change and obesity should be performed annually by calculating BMI in adults with Down syndrome; the USPSTF behavioral weight loss interventions to prevent obesity-related morbidity and mortality in adults should be followed.

In asymptomatic adults with Down syndrome, routine cervical spine radiographs should not be used to screen for risk of spinal cord injury. Instead, annual screening of adults with Down syndrome should include signs and symptoms of cervical myelopathy using targeted history and physical examination.

For primary prevention of osteoporotic fractures in adults with Down syndrome, there is insufficient evidence to recommend for or against applying established osteoporosis screening guidelines, including fracture risk estimation; thus, good clinical practice would support a shared decision-making approach.

All adults with Down syndrome who sustain a fragility fracture should be evaluated for secondary causes of osteoporosis, including screening for hyperthyroidism, celiac disease, vitamin D deficiency, hyperparathyroidism, and medications associated with adverse effects on bone health.
Screen adults with Down syndrome for hypothyroidism every 1-2 years using a serum thyrotropin test beginning at age 21.
With improving social support and medical interventions, life expectancy is increasing for patients with Down syndrome in developed nations. B
Some adults with Down syndrome can live independently with the increasing number of available group homes and employment opportunities for people with disabilities. C

Life expectancy is increasing for patients with Down syndrome in developing nations. A recent population-based study in the United States yielded a median age at death of 49 years, although ages at death as high as 60 years have been reported in other developed countries.
Alzheimer's disease and its complications are the leading cause of death in adults with Down syndrome.

In a population study of 16,506 infants with Down syndrome delivered during 1983 to 2003, the overall 1-month and 1-, 5-, and 20-year survival probabilities were 98%, 93%, 91%, and 88% respectively. Presence of a heart defect increased the risk of death in the post neonatal period nearly fivefold (adjusted HR 4.6; 95% CI 3.9-5.4) and was one of the most significant predictors of mortality through age 20 years. Similarly, a European cohort study showed the 10-year survival in patients with Down syndrome was relatively high: 98% in those without cardiac or digestive anomalies, 92% in those with cardiac anomalies, 93% in those with digestive anomalies, and 89% in those with both. Over the past 40 years, the difference in 5-year survival between children with Down syndrome with and without congenital heart defects has improved.
In a Japanese population registry study, the age at death among people with Down syndrome increased over 20 years to over 1 in 3 persons (36.6%) living to age 60 years or more in 2016.

Using a national database of acute hospitalizations in northern England comparing 558 people with Down syndrome to an age- and gender-matched control group of 5580 people, respiratory failure was the sole risk factor for mortality in the Down syndrome population (relative risk 9.791; 95% CI 1.6-59.9).

Children with Down syndrome have a 10- to 20-fold increased risk of developing leukemia, with the highest risk occurring before age 5 years. Up to 10% of infants with Down syndrome will develop a transient leukemoid reaction with an approximate overall survival of 85%. GATA1 mutations appear to be the leukaemogenic source for this condition. Approximately 20% of infants who manifest this transient leukemoid reaction will go on to develop acute leukemia.

In some individuals with Down syndrome, there is a loss of previously acquired adaptive, cognitive, and social functioning that most often occurs in adolescence to early adulthood. This has been called Down syndrome Disintegrative Disorder or simply referred to as regression. This condition has a subacute onset with mood lability, decreased participation in activities of daily living, new-onset insomnia, social withdrawal, autistic-like regression, mutism, and catatonia followed by a chronic phase in which baseline functioning may not return to normal. There are no clear diagnostic criteria or definitive testing, although a medical and psychosocial evaluation is recommended.

In a case series of 35 patients with Down syndrome and regression, investigators noted four times as many mental health concerns, six times as many stressors, and seven times as many depressive symptoms. Medical evaluation of these patients revealed some cases with abnormalities in vitamin D 25-OH levels, polysomnograms, thyroid peroxidase antibodies, and celiac screens.

Common comorbidities in patients with Down syndrome are noted in the section on other impact. In one study of community dwelling adults with Down syndrome at a mean age of 38.3 years, 374/421 (88.8%) had multimorbidity with the most prevalent conditions being visual impairment (72.9%), thyroid disease (50.1%) and hearing impairment (26.8%). Polypharmacy was observed in 10.5% of the patients.

In a study of psychiatric comorbidities over the lifespan in 602 individuals with Down syndrome in England and Wales, standardized morbidity ratios which compared observed to expected rates in the general population were increased in males and decreased in females for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and anxiety and increased in both males and females with Down syndrome for dementia, autism, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, and depression. Over time, receptive language abilities increasingly deviated from age-typical levels, with males scoring more poorly than females. Most health co-morbidities were not associated with poorer cognitive function with the exception of autism and epilepsy.
Adults with Down syndrome can live more independently due to the increasing availability of group homes and employment programs for people with disabilities.
See and discussion under "Diagnostic Testing" for guidance regarding routine surveillance of pediatric pateints with Down syndrome.
Use GLOBAL Medical Care Guidelines for Adults with Down Syndrome Checklist to support the health of adults with Down syndrome directly or through their caregivers.

Authors of older case report and review identified 30 pregnancies in 26 mothers with Down syndrome resulting in 10 children with Down syndrome, 10 children without Down syndrome, 6 children with some form of physical or cognitive abnormality, 1 set of preterm but nonviable twins, 1 stillbirth, and 2 spontaneous abortions.

In a systematic review of 23 studies, women with a disability (pooled unadjusted OR 1.45, 95% CI 1.16-1.82) and intellectual and developmental disabilities (pooled unadjusted OR 1.77, 95% CI 1.21-2.60) had increased risk for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. In addition, women with any (pooled unadjusted OR 1.31, 95% CI 1.02-1.68), physical (pooled unadjusted OR 1.60, 95% CI 1.21-2.13), and intellectual and developmental disabilities (pooled unadjusted OR 1.29, 95% CI 1.02-1.63) also had increased risk for cesarean delivery.

feature.caption: Recommended Health Supervision Screening for Down Syndrome.*
feature.feature_body:
Test Frequency
Hearing (audiology evaluation) At 6 months, then annually with behavioral audiogram. Refer to ENT
Cardiology referral for echocardiogram Newborn period (birth to 1 month)
CBC (screen for leukemoid reaction, leukemia, polycythemia ); iron; hemoglobin Newborn period. Iron annually, ages 1-13 years. Hbg, annually ages 13-21 years
Thyroid-stimulating hormone Newborn period, 6 months, 12 months,then annually
Celiac screening 1 yeas and as indicated by symptoms (screen at health maintenance visits)
Ophthalmologic evaluation Birth and 6 months of age (cataract); refer for annual exam ages 1-5 years, every 2-3 years after
Atlantoaxial instability Discuss cervical spine-positioning precautions/contact sports at least biennially; x-ray if symptoms
Sleep apnea-specific history Annually, sleep study by age 4 years
Dental evaluation After tooth eruption, reassure about delayed erpution at 1 year
*See full report for anticipatory guidance recommendations.From American Academy of Pediatrics. Committee on Genetics. American Academy of Pediatrics: Health supervision for children with Down syndrome. Pediatrics 2011;128(2):393-406.
